missions.name: African-initiated churches and prophets (Harris, Kimbangu, Aladura, Shembe)
missions.statusNote: Active and numerous, though increasingly overshadowed since the 1980s by newer Pentecostal-charismatic churches. Several (Kimbanguists, Church of the Lord Aladura, and others) joined the World Council of Churches, and the Organization of African Instituted Churches (1978) gives the movement a common voice; the Zion Christian Church and the Shembe churches remain among the largest religious bodies in southern Africa.
missions.summary: From the 1880s onward Africans founded churches of their own, first by seceding from mission churches over racism and control (the ‘Ethiopian’ churches), then through prophets such as William Wade Harris, Garrick Braide, Simon Kimbangu, Isaiah Shembe, Engenas Lekganyane, Joseph Babalola and Josiah Oshitelu, who preached repentance, burned charms, healed by prayer and gathered hundreds of thousands into churches led entirely by Africans. These ‘African Initiated’ (or Independent, or Instituted) Churches translated Christianity into African idioms of healing, prophecy, dreams and communal ritual, and became the first large-scale proof that the faith could flourish beyond missionary control.
missions.story:
The first African-initiated churches were protests. In Lagos in 1888 members of the American Southern Baptist congregation left to form the Native Baptist Church; in 1891 Anglicans unhappy with missionary control formed the United Native African Church; and the humiliation of Bishop Samuel Ajayi Crowther, whose Niger Mission was dismantled by young CMS missionaries in 1890–91, became a lasting symbol of why Africans might need churches of their own. In South Africa the Wesleyan minister Mangena Mokone founded the Ethiopian Church in Pretoria in 1892, taking the name from Psalm 68:31 (‘Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God’). These ‘Ethiopian’ churches usually kept mission doctrine and liturgy but insisted on African leadership; the Swedish missionary-bishop Bengt Sundkler later distinguished them from the ‘Zionist’ type, which reshaped worship itself.

The second wave was prophetic. In 1910, imprisoned in Liberia, the Grebo teacher William Wade Harris experienced a vision of the Archangel Gabriel; in 1913–14 he walked barefoot along the coast of the French Ivory Coast into the British Gold Coast in a white gown, carrying a cross, a Bible and a calabash. In roughly eighteen months he baptised perhaps 100,000–120,000 people, ordered fetishes burned, preached the Sabbath and the Ten Commandments, tolerated polygamy and told converts to wait for teachers ‘with the Book’. The French deported him in 1914–15, but his converts built chapels and waited; when the Wesleyan missionary William Platt arrived in 1924 he found tens of thousands ready to become Methodists, while others formed the Harrist Church. In the Niger Delta, Garrick Braide’s healing revival (1915–16) produced the Christ Army Church after the Anglicans disowned him and the colonial government jailed him.

In the Belgian Congo, Simon Kimbangu, a Baptist catechist trained by the Baptist Missionary Society, began healing at Nkamba in April 1921. Crowds abandoned mission stations and plantations; the colonial state, fearing insurrection, arrested him within months. Sentenced to death, commuted to life, he spent thirty years in prison at Élisabethville (Lubumbashi), dying there in 1951. His followers, persecuted and deported for decades, emerged as the Église de Jésus-Christ sur la Terre par son envoyé spécial Simon Kimbangu, officially recognised on the eve of independence in 1959 and admitted to the World Council of Churches in 1969. In South Africa, Isaiah Shembe founded the amaNazaretha (Nazareth Baptist Church) in 1910 at Ekuphakameni near Durban, composing hymns, instituting a Saturday Sabbath and an annual pilgrimage to the mountain Nhlangakazi; Engenas Lekganyane, drawing on the Zionist movement that had come from John Alexander Dowie’s Zion City, Illinois, founded the Zion Christian Church around 1924, whose Easter gatherings at Moria now draw crowds counted in the hundreds of thousands to over a million.

In western Nigeria the influenza pandemic of 1918 gave rise to prayer groups (the ‘Precious Stone’ society at Ijebu-Ode) which rejected Western medicine and practised healing by prayer — hence the Yoruba name Aladura, ‘owners of prayer’. Moses Orimolade and the young visionary Christiana Abiodun Akinsowon founded the Cherubim and Seraphim in Lagos in 1925; Josiah Oshitelu founded the Church of the Lord (Aladura) at Ogere in 1930; and in the same year Joseph Ayo Babalola’s revival at Ilesha brought mass conversions and, after a failed partnership with the British Apostolic Church (broken partly over the use of medicine), the Christ Apostolic Church (1941). Samuel Oshoffa’s Celestial Church of Christ, founded at Porto-Novo in Dahomey in 1947, spread back into Nigeria and later to the diaspora in Europe and North America.

These churches agreed with the missions on much: the Bible (often in translation made by missionaries), the Trinity in most cases, the rejection of ancestral shrines and charms, baptism and the authority of Christ. They disagreed over who held authority, how the Spirit was experienced and what African custom could be kept. Many accepted polygamous converts, used drums and dance, white garments, holy water and sacred sites, and gave prophets, visions and healing a central role. Missionaries and many African Protestants long called them ‘syncretistic’ or ‘nativistic’; scholars such as Bengt Sundkler, Harold Turner, J. D. Y. Peel, Allan Anderson and Kwame Bediako later argued that most were authentic attempts to read the Bible through African questions about evil, misfortune and healing, while acknowledging that some movements did drift into messianism around the founder.

After independence the movement grew and diversified. In Zimbabwe the Johane Masowe and Johane Marange apostolic churches (from 1932) gathered huge followings; in Kenya the Akurinu and Legio Maria (1963) arose; in Zambia Alice Lenshina’s Lumpa Church ended in a tragic armed confrontation with the new state in 1964. Estimates of membership vary widely, but by the late twentieth century African Initiated Churches were commonly counted in the tens of millions across the continent. Since the 1980s, newer Pentecostal and charismatic churches have drawn many younger urban Africans away from the white-garment churches, often criticising them as mixed with traditional religion, while themselves adopting much that the AICs pioneered — healing, deliverance, prophecy and African leadership.
beliefs: The Bible, read directly and often literally in vernacular translation, as the authority above missionary tradition and denominational custom.

God’s power over witchcraft, evil spirits and misfortune, shown through healing by prayer, holy water and the laying on of hands rather than (in many Aladura and Zionist churches) through Western medicine.
The continuing gift of prophecy, visions and dreams, so that God speaks to African prophets as he did to Old Testament prophets.
Strong Old Testament emphases: the Sabbath in some churches, food and purity laws, sacred mountains and pilgrimage, and the founder as a Moses- or Elijah-like figure.
Rejection of ancestral shrines, charms and ‘fetishes’, often more radical than the mission churches, combined with acceptance of some customs (polygamy, drums, dance) that missions forbade.
In some movements, a high or messianic view of the founder (Shembe among the amaNazaretha, Kimbangu in later Kimbanguist teaching), which other Christians regard as a departure from orthodoxy.
strategies: Itinerant prophets who walked from village to village calling for repentance, burning charms and baptising whole communities, as Harris did along the Ivory Coast in 1913–15.
Healing services and prayer camps that met urgent needs left unaddressed by mission medicine and colonial health services.
Indigenous hymnody, dance, drumming and white robes that made worship recognisably African and easy to transmit orally.
Holy cities and pilgrimage centres (Nkamba, Ekuphakameni, Moria, Ogere, Ilesha) that gave dispersed members a shared sacred geography.
Lay and charismatic leadership, including women prophets, without the long seminary training and missionary approval required by mission churches.
Migration networks that carried the churches to the mines and cities of southern Africa and later to London, Paris and North America.
groupsReached: Coastal peoples of Côte d’Ivoire and western Ghana (Adjukru, Alladian, Ebrié, Nzima and others) through Harris’s preaching of 1913–15.
The Bakongo of the Lower Congo, among whom Kimbanguism became a mass movement despite decades of colonial repression.
Yoruba communities of western Nigeria and Benin through the Aladura churches.
Zulu-speaking peoples of Natal through Shembe’s amaNazaretha.
Northern Sotho, Pedi and migrant mine workers across South Africa, Zimbabwe and Botswana through the Zion Christian Church and other Zionist churches.
Shona-speaking Zimbabweans through the vaPostori (apostolic) churches of Johane Masowe and Johane Marange.
African migrants in Britain, France and the United States, among whom Cherubim and Seraphim, Celestial and Christ Apostolic congregations were founded from the 1960s.
challenges: Colonial repression: Harris was deported, Braide jailed, Kimbangu imprisoned for thirty years and tens of thousands of his followers deported to distant parts of the Congo.
Hostility or condescension from mission churches, which often disciplined members who joined them and labelled them ‘sects’ or ‘syncretist’.
Limited theological education, which made it hard to train leaders and to answer charges of heterodoxy.
Succession disputes on the death of founders, which split the amaNazaretha, the Zion Christian Church and others into rival branches.
Competition since the 1980s from Pentecostal and charismatic churches that appeal to younger, urban and educated Africans.
The difficulty of applying healing teaching amid HIV/AIDS and other epidemics without discouraging medical treatment.
harms: Some churches forbade medicine and hospital treatment, with documented cases of preventable deaths, especially of children, in faith-healing communities.
Witch-finding and accusations made by some prophets stigmatised vulnerable people, particularly elderly women and children.
Founder-centred teaching sometimes turned into messianism and the cult of a ruling family, with church property and authority passed down hereditary lines.
Alice Lenshina’s Lumpa Church, withdrawing from the state, clashed with Zambian nationalists and troops in 1964; several hundred people died on all sides.
Acceptance of polygamy and of the prophet’s authority over marriage sometimes entrenched the subordination of women and child marriage in particular communities.
developments: Demonstrated, decades before decolonisation, that Africans could lead, finance and multiply churches without missionary control.
Created a large body of African Christian hymnody, liturgy and ritual, such as Shembe’s hymns, which is now studied as a major religious literature.
Anticipated and shaped African Pentecostalism’s emphasis on healing, deliverance and prophecy, and its engagement with the spirit world.
Provided mutual aid, moral discipline (abstinence from alcohol and tobacco) and community for migrants and the urban poor.
Prompted African theologians (Mbiti, Bediako, Oduyoye) and Western scholars to rethink ‘syncretism’ and to treat African culture as a vehicle for the gospel.
Gave Africa an early ecumenical voice through WCC membership (Kimbanguists 1969) and the Organization of African Instituted Churches (1978).
missions.outcome: African Initiated Churches proved that Christianity in Africa did not depend on missionaries, and they prepared the ground for the explosive growth of African Christianity after 1960. They remain a large and distinctive family, though many members have moved to newer Pentecostal churches.

keyPeople.name: William Wade Harris
keyPeople.focus: Preached across the Ivory Coast and western Gold Coast in 1913–15, baptising perhaps 100,000 or more.
keyPeople.outcome: Deported by the French; his converts became Methodists, Catholics or members of the Harrist Church.

keyPeople.name: Simon Kimbangu
keyPeople.focus: Healing ministry of 1921 that drew crowds from mission stations.
keyPeople.outcome: Imprisoned for thirty years; the Kimbanguist Church became one of Africa’s largest independent churches.

keyPeople.name: Isaiah Shembe
keyPeople.role: Prophet, hymn-writer and founder of the amaNazaretha
keyPeople.focus: Founded the Nazareth Baptist Church in 1910 with Sabbath worship, pilgrimage and Zulu hymnody.
keyPeople.outcome: His church continues under rival branches led by his descendants.

keyPeople.name: Joseph Ayo Babalola
keyPeople.focus: Led the 1930 Ilesha revival of healing and mass conversion.
keyPeople.outcome: Revered as spiritual founder of the Christ Apostolic Church.

keyPeople.name: Moses Orimolade Tunolase and Christiana Abiodun Akinsowon
keyPeople.role: Founders of the Cherubim and Seraphim
keyPeople.focus: Prayer, visions and healing among Lagos Yoruba from 1925.
keyPeople.outcome: The movement fragmented into many branches but spread across Nigeria and the diaspora.

keyPeople.name: Engenas Lekganyane
keyPeople.role: Founder of the Zion Christian Church
keyPeople.focus: Healing, purity rules and the holy city of Moria.
keyPeople.outcome: The ZCC became the largest independent church in southern Africa.

keyPeople.name: Josiah Olunowo Oshitelu
keyPeople.role: Founder of the Church of the Lord (Aladura)
keyPeople.focus: Prophetic visions and a written ‘holy script’; founded his church in 1930.
keyPeople.outcome: The church spread to Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ghana and Britain and joined the WCC in 1975.

keyPeople.name: Garrick Sokari Braide
keyPeople.focus: Healing and anti-charm revival in the Delta in 1915–16.
keyPeople.outcome: Jailed by the British; his followers formed the Christ Army Church.

countries.text: Birthplace of the earliest secessions (Native Baptist Church 1888, United Native African Church 1891) and of the Aladura movement after 1918, including the Cherubim and Seraphim, the Church of the Lord and the Christ Apostolic Church.
Home of the Ethiopian churches (Mokone, 1892) and of the Zionist family, including Shembe’s amaNazaretha (1910) and the Zion Christian Church (c. 1924).
Scene of Harris’s mass baptisms of 1913–14 and seat of the Harrist Church.
Harris preached around Axim and Apollonia in 1914; later many independent and spiritual churches arose, including the Musama Disco Christo Church (1922).
Harris’s homeland, where his prophetic call came in prison in 1910.
Kimbangu’s healing movement and the persecuted Kimbanguist Church, recognised in 1959 and now one of Africa’s largest independent churches.
Samuel Oshoffa founded the Celestial Church of Christ at Porto-Novo in 1947.
The vaPostori apostolic churches of Johane Masowe and Johane Marange, recognisable by white robes and open-air worship, grew from 1932.
Akurinu (Arathi) prophets arose among the Kikuyu from the late 1920s, and Legio Maria broke from Catholicism among the Luo in 1963; Nairobi hosts the Organization of African Instituted Churches.
Alice Lenshina’s Lumpa Church grew rapidly in the 1950s before its violent suppression in 1964.
Aladura churches (Church of the Lord, Cherubim and Seraphim, Celestial Church) were established in London from the 1960s among West African migrants and students.

journeys.title: Prophet Harris’s walk along the Ivory Coast and Gold Coast
journeys.people: William Wade Harris with women companions Helen Valentine and Mary Pioka
journeys.text: Wearing a white gown and carrying a cross, Bible and calabash, Harris walked eastward along the coast, baptising whole villages and ordering charms burned. After a few months in the Gold Coast he returned to the Ivory Coast, where the French authorities arrested and expelled him in late 1914 / early 1915.

journeys.title: Simon Kimbangu: from Nkamba to prison in Élisabethville
journeys.text: After six months of healing ministry, Kimbangu was arrested in September 1921, sentenced to death (commuted by the Belgian king to life imprisonment) and taken some 2,000 km across the colony to Élisabethville, where he died in prison in 1951. Nkamba later became the Kimbanguist holy city, ‘New Jerusalem’.

journeys.title: The amaNazaretha pilgrimage to Nhlangakazi
journeys.text: Shembe instituted an annual January pilgrimage to the holy mountain Nhlangakazi, which he had climbed in obedience to a vision; the pilgrimage, with hymn-singing and sacred dance, remains the movement’s central rite.

relations.text: AIC migrants founded churches in Europe and North America from the 1960s, an early form of ‘reverse mission’.
The Kimbanguist Church (1969) and the Church of the Lord (Aladura) (1975) joined the World Council of Churches, which also supported AIC theological education.
Babalola’s movement affiliated with the British Apostolic Church in the 1930s and Zionist churches grew from Dowie- and Pentecostal-linked missions, though both relationships ended in separation.

agreements.text: Shared the conviction that Africans must have the Bible in their own languages; vernacular Scripture was the seedbed of nearly every prophet movement.
Agreed on healing, prophecy, spiritual warfare and the immediacy of the Holy Spirit, which is why many scholars treat AICs as part of the wider Pentecostal-type family.
Echoed Henry Venn’s ideal of self-governing, self-supporting and self-propagating churches, which the CMS itself had abandoned after Crowther.

disagreements.text: The dismantling of Bishop Crowther’s Niger Mission in 1890–91 and missionary racism drove Nigerian Anglicans into the first African churches.
BMS and other Protestant missions in the Congo distanced themselves from Kimbangu in 1921 and disciplined members who followed him; reconciliation came only much later.
Babalola’s followers broke with the British Apostolic Church (1939–41) partly because the missionaries accepted medicine and quinine, which the Nigerians held contrary to faith healing.
Evangelical faith missions often regarded the white-garment churches as syncretistic and refused fellowship over polygamy, holy water and founder-veneration.

deviations: Later Kimbanguist teaching identified Simon Kimbangu with the Holy Spirit (the promised Paraclete) and treated his sons as divine figures, a departure from historic Trinitarian doctrine that strained relations with other Protestants and the WCC.
Some amaNazaretha hymns and teaching present Shembe as a messianic intermediary for black people, which critics regard as replacing Christ.
Bans on all medicine in some Aladura and Zionist churches went beyond the founders’ emphasis on prayer and caused avoidable suffering.
Succession by heredity and the accumulation of wealth by prophet families moved some churches away from their founders’ ascetic simplicity.

missions.name: Korean revival and the Korean missionary movement (1907 Pyongyang, Korea as a sending nation)
missions.statusNote: Active: South Korea is one of the world’s largest sending nations, with around 20,000–22,000 long-term missionaries reported by the Korea World Missions Association through the 2010s and 2020s. Church growth at home has plateaued since the 1990s amid scandals, denominational division and secularisation, and Christianity in North Korea survives only underground.
missions.summary: Korean Christianity was unusual from the start: Catholicism was brought home by Korean scholars in 1784 before any foreign priest arrived, and Protestantism spread through Bibles translated in Manchuria by Koreans and Scots before resident missionaries landed in 1885. Adopting the Nevius plan of self-support and Bible study, and set alight by the Pyongyang Great Revival of 1907, the Korean church became strongly self-propagating, sent its own missionaries from 1907, endured Japanese colonial rule, the Shinto shrine crisis, war and division, and after 1970 grew into a global missionary force — while also exporting megachurch, prosperity and highly competitive styles of ministry.
missions.story:
Christianity reached Korea through Korean initiative. Confucian scholars studying Catholic books written in Chinese by Matteo Ricci and other Jesuits sent Yi Seung-hun to Beijing, where he was baptised in 1784; returning home he baptised others, and a lay-led Catholic church existed for a decade before the first priest, the Chinese Zhou Wenmo, arrived in 1795. Refusal of ancestor rites brought fierce persecution in 1801, 1839, 1846 and above all 1866, when perhaps 8,000 Catholics were killed. Protestantism came by a similar route: in Mukden (Shenyang) the Scottish missionary John Ross and Korean helpers translated the Gospels (New Testament 1887), and colporteurs such as Seo Sang-ryun carried them across the border, gathering a believing community at Sorae in Hwanghae before any Protestant missionary resided in Korea.

The American Presbyterian doctor Horace Allen arrived in 1884, and the Presbyterian Horace Underwood and the Methodist Henry Appenzeller landed at Chemulpo (Incheon) at Easter 1885. In 1890 the Presbyterian missionaries invited John Nevius from Shandong, and adopted his plan: Korean believers would support their own pastors and buildings, evangelise their neighbours and study the Bible systematically in winter Bible classes. Missionaries did much — hospitals (Severance), schools (Ewha, Yonsei’s forerunners, Pai Chai), the promotion of the vernacular Hangul script — but the method placed responsibility on Koreans from the beginning.

The Great Revival broke out at the Jangdaehyun (Central) Church in Pyongyang during the winter Bible class of January 1907. After elder Gil Seon-ju and others publicly confessed sins, waves of weeping, confession and reconciliation spread through the city and across the peninsula; the practices of daybreak prayer (saebyeok gido) and unison audible prayer (tongseong gido) that still mark Korean Protestantism date from this era. The same year the first seven Korean Presbyterian ministers were ordained and the new presbytery sent Yi Ki-pung as missionary to Jeju Island; in 1912 the General Assembly was organised, and in 1913 it sent three Korean missionaries to Laiyang in Shandong, China. Koreans also followed emigrants to Japan, Manchuria, Siberia, Hawaii and California.

Under Japanese rule (1910–45) Christianity became tied to Korean national identity. Sixteen of the thirty-three signatories of the 1919 March First independence declaration were Christians, and churches suffered reprisals such as the Jeam-ri massacre. In the 1930s the authorities demanded worship at Shinto shrines; in 1938 the Presbyterian General Assembly, under police pressure, declared shrine worship a civic act, while resisters such as the pastor Ju Gi-cheol died in prison (1944). After liberation, quarrels over this compromise split the Presbyterians (the Koshin church, 1952), and further divisions followed over biblical criticism (Kijang, 1953) and membership of the World Council of Churches (Tonghap and Hapdong, 1959). The communist north, where Pyongyang had been called the ‘Jerusalem of the East’, drove Christians south or underground.

In the decades of industrialisation after the Korean War the churches grew dramatically: Protestants rose from a few hundred thousand in 1950 to about 6.5 million in the 1985 census and about 9.7 million (19.7%) in 2015, with Catholics another 3.9 million. Mass rallies (Billy Graham’s Seoul crusade of 1973, Explo ’74) and cell-group megachurches such as David Yonggi Cho’s Yoido Full Gospel Church, founded in a tent in 1958 with Choi Ja-sil and later claiming over 700,000 members, made Seoul a showcase of church growth. Cho’s ‘threefold blessing’ (spiritual, physical and material, drawn from 3 John 2) was widely criticised as a prosperity gospel; at the same time minjung theologians such as Ahn Byung-mu and many Christians stood with workers and the democracy movement against military rule.

From the late 1970s Korean missionaries went abroad in rapidly rising numbers — fewer than a hundred in 1979, about 1,600 by 1990, about 8,000 by 2000 and over 20,000 by the 2010s — to China, the Philippines, Japan, Central Asia, Russia, Africa, Latin America and the Muslim world. Korean missions mobilised churches, prayer and short-term teams with remarkable energy, but also met criticism for planting Korean denominational structures abroad, competition between agencies, paternalism toward local churches and risky evangelism, made vivid when twenty-three volunteers from Saemmul Church were kidnapped by the Taliban in Afghanistan in 2007 and two were killed. In 2024 the Fourth Lausanne Congress met at Incheon, symbolising Korea’s place at the centre of global evangelical mission.
beliefs: Evangelical Protestant conviction of the Bible’s authority, conversion and the necessity of evangelism, fixed early by missionaries largely of conservative Presbyterian and Methodist outlook.
Fervent, disciplined prayer — daybreak prayer, all-night prayer, prayer mountains and unison spoken prayer — as the engine of revival.
Public repentance and moral reform, including abstinence from alcohol and tobacco and the rejection of ancestor rites.
Strict Sunday observance and tithing as marks of a committed believer.
A strong sense that Korea, a small and suffering nation, has been called to carry the gospel to the world, often expressed as a debt to the missionaries it received.
In Pentecostal and charismatic streams, Spirit baptism, healing and Cho’s ‘fivefold gospel and threefold blessing’.
strategies: The Nevius plan: self-supporting congregations, Korean-funded pastors and buildings, and evangelism by every believer.
Winter and summer Bible classes and later Bible study cell groups, which trained a literate lay leadership.
Use of the Hangul script for Bibles, hymns and tracts, making literacy and faith spread together.
Institution-building: hospitals, mission schools and universities such as Yonsei and Ewha, which shaped modern Korean elites.
Cell-group (home group) systems and mass rallies that allowed megachurches to grow without losing pastoral oversight.
Denominational and church-based mission sending, short-term teams, diaspora churches and partnership through the Korea World Missions Association (1990).
groupsReached: Northern provincial towns and the commercial class of Pyongyang and Pyongan, where Protestantism first became a mass movement.
Women, who were reached by ‘Bible women’ and girls’ schools and became the backbone of Korean congregations.
Urban migrants and the poor of Seoul during the rapid industrialisation of the 1960s–80s.
Korean diaspora communities in Japan, Manchuria, Central Asia (Koryo-saram), the United States and later worldwide.
Chinese in Shandong from 1913, and after 1992 many Chinese and ethnic Korean Chinese through often covert work in China.
Peoples of the Philippines, Mongolia, Cambodia, Russia, Central Asia, Africa and the Middle East through post-1980 missions.
challenges: Persecution of Catholics in 1801–66, Japanese colonial pressure and the shrine-worship crisis of the 1930s.
The partition of Korea and the Korean War (1950–53), which destroyed the northern church and created a refugee church in the south.
Repeated schisms, leaving well over a hundred Presbyterian denominations in South Korea.
Security and legal risks for missionaries in China, Central Asia and the Muslim world, including expulsions, kidnappings and killings.
Declining growth and rising public distrust since the 1990s, with many young people leaving the churches.
Ageing missionaries, burnout and inadequate member care after the rapid growth of the 1990s and 2000s.
harms: The 1938 Presbyterian acceptance of Shinto shrine worship and wartime collaboration with the Japanese empire, for which the church later repented.
Prosperity and success teaching in some megachurches, which tied faith to material blessing and fuelled a church-growth competition.
Financial and leadership scandals, including the 2014 conviction of David Yonggi Cho for breach of trust and hereditary succession of megachurch pulpits (such as Myungsung Church, 2017).
Aggressive or culturally insensitive evangelism abroad, including the planting of Korean denominational structures and rivalry between Korean agencies in the same fields.
Anti-communist and nationalist politics in parts of the church, including support for authoritarian regimes in the 1960s–70s.
Breakaway movements with controversial founders (the Unification Church, Shincheonji and others) that damaged the public reputation of Christianity.
developments: One of the clearest early examples of a self-supporting, self-propagating and self-governing church in Asia.
Major contributions to modern Korean education, medicine, women’s advancement and Hangul literacy.
A vital tradition of prayer — daybreak prayer, prayer mountains, tongseong gido — now practised by Korean churches worldwide.
Christian participation in the independence movement (1919) and later in the democracy and labour movements.
Korea’s emergence as one of the world’s largest missionary-sending countries, inspiring other Asian churches.
Hosting the Fourth Lausanne Congress (Incheon, 2024) and contributing Korean theologians to global debates.
missions.outcome: From a self-evangelised Catholic community and a Bible-translated Protestant church, Korea became both one of Asia’s most Christian societies (about 28% Christian in 2015) and a major sending nation, though its domestic church now faces stagnation and a crisis of public trust.

keyPeople.name: Yi Seung-hun (Peter)
keyPeople.focus: Baptised in Beijing in 1784; founded a lay Catholic community on his return.
keyPeople.outcome: Martyred in the persecution of 1801.

keyPeople.name: Seo Sang-ryun
keyPeople.focus: Helped John Ross translate the Gospels in Manchuria and gathered the Sorae congregation.
keyPeople.outcome: Remembered as founder of one of the first Protestant congregations in Korea.

keyPeople.name: Horace G. Underwood
keyPeople.origin: London; raised in the United States
keyPeople.focus: Church planting, Bible translation and founding of what became Yonsei University.
keyPeople.outcome: Arrived at Easter 1885; died in 1916.

keyPeople.name: Henry G. Appenzeller
keyPeople.focus: Founded Pai Chai school and Chungdong First Methodist Church; Bible translation.
keyPeople.outcome: Drowned in 1902 while travelling to a translators’ meeting.

keyPeople.name: Gil Seon-ju
keyPeople.focus: Leading voice in the 1907 revival and originator of organised daybreak prayer.
keyPeople.outcome: One of the first seven Korean ministers; signatory of the 1919 independence declaration.

keyPeople.name: Ju Gi-cheol (Chu Ki-chol)
keyPeople.focus: Refused Shinto shrine worship.
keyPeople.outcome: Died in prison in 1944; honoured as a martyr.

keyPeople.name: David Yonggi Cho
keyPeople.role: Founder of Yoido Full Gospel Church
keyPeople.focus: Pentecostal preaching, cell groups and the ‘threefold blessing’.
keyPeople.outcome: Built one of the world’s largest congregations; convicted of breach of trust in 2014.

keyPeople.name: Ahn Byung-mu
keyPeople.focus: Read the Gospels from the standpoint of the suffering people (minjung).
keyPeople.outcome: Imprisoned under military rule; shaped Korean and Asian contextual theology.

countries.text: Lay-founded Catholic church (1784) and Protestant church (1880s); the Pyongyang revival of 1907 and post-war growth made South Korea a centre of world Christianity.
John Ross and Korean helpers translated the Bible at Mukden; Korean Christians later followed emigrants into Manchuria.
The Korean Presbyterian General Assembly sent three missionaries to Laiyang, an early cross-cultural mission from an Asian church.
Korean Christian students and workers founded churches in Tokyo and among Koreans in Japan from 1906.
Korean labourers in Hawaii founded churches from 1903, beginning a diaspora church now numbering thousands of congregations.
Became one of the largest fields of Korean missionaries, focusing on church planting, schools and theological training.
After the Soviet collapse Korean missionaries worked among the ethnic Korean Koryo-saram and other peoples of Russia, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.
The kidnapping of twenty-three Saemmul Church volunteers by the Taliban prompted a national debate about the risks and ethics of short-term mission.

journeys.title: Seo Sang-ryun carries the Ross Gospels from Manchuria into Korea
journeys.people: Seo Sang-ryun and other Korean colporteurs
journeys.text: Korean helpers of John Ross smuggled newly printed Hangul Gospels across the Yalu and gathered believers at Uiju and Sorae, so that when Underwood arrived there were already Koreans asking for baptism.

journeys.title: Underwood and Appenzeller sail to Korea
journeys.people: Horace G. Underwood, Henry and Ella Appenzeller
journeys.text: The two missionaries landed together at Chemulpo on Easter Sunday, 5 April 1885, after preparing in Japan, where the Korean convert Yi Su-jeong had translated Mark’s Gospel.

journeys.title: Korean Presbyterian missionaries to Shandong
journeys.people: Pak Tae-ro, Sa Byeong-sun and Kim Yeong-hun
journeys.text: Sent by the new General Assembly as its first foreign mission, the Korean missionaries worked in Laiyang county alongside American Presbyterians; the mission continued until the Communist victory of 1949.

relations.text: Korea’s post-1980 sending movement became the model and catalyst for many Asian and other majority-world missions.
Korean churches were prominent in Lausanne gatherings and hosted the Fourth Lausanne Congress at Incheon in 2024.
Korean megachurches, especially Yoido, were studied as showcases of church growth and cell-group methods.

agreements.text: Embodied the three-self ideal of Venn and Anderson through the Nevius plan, adopted in 1890.
Shared the evangelical, Bible-centred and conversion-focused piety of the faith missions, as well as the CIM’s stress on prayer.
Embraced the Lausanne priority of evangelism and the unreached-peoples strategy of the 1980s–90s.

disagreements.text: Conflict over membership of the World Council of Churches split the Presbyterian Church of Korea in 1959 into the ecumenical Tonghap and the conservative Hapdong.
Early Korean Catholics, following Rome’s ruling against the Chinese Rites, rejected ancestor rites that Ricci’s followers had tolerated — the issue that provoked the persecutions.
Korean missionaries in China have often worked with unregistered house churches, causing friction with the Three-Self churches and Chinese authorities.

deviations: The acceptance of Shinto shrine worship in 1938 departed from the church’s own confessional commitments, as Korean Presbyterians later acknowledged.
Prosperity and success teaching in some megachurches moved away from the revival’s original stress on repentance and suffering.
Competitive church growth and hereditary succession of pulpits contradicted the self-giving ethos of the early Korean church.
New religious movements born in Korean Protestant milieus, such as the Unification Church and Shincheonji, departed from orthodox Christology altogether.

missions.name: Chinese indigenous and house churches (Watchman Nee, John Sung, Three-Self, Back to Jerusalem)
missions.statusNote: Active but divided between the state-registered Three-Self/China Christian Council churches and a large, diverse unregistered house-church sector. Since 2018 tighter religious regulations and a ‘sinicisation’ campaign have closed prominent urban congregations and restricted online and youth ministry.
missions.summary: From the early twentieth century Chinese Christians sought to free their churches from missionary control and foreign stigma. Independent churches, the True Jesus Church, the Jesus Family and Watchman Nee’s ‘Little Flock’ (Local Churches), the revival preaching of John Sung and the uncompromising Wang Mingdao created a Chinese Protestantism that survived the expulsion of missionaries after 1949. The Communist state organised the Three-Self Patriotic Movement in 1950–54; those who refused it formed the house churches, which endured the Cultural Revolution and grew after 1979 into one of the largest Christian populations in Asia, with a visionary if largely unrealised ‘Back to Jerusalem’ missionary dream.
missions.story:
Chinese Protestantism was born under the shadow of the unequal treaties, and many Chinese saw Christianity as a foreign religion protected by gunboats; the Boxer violence of 1900, in which tens of thousands of Chinese Christians and some two hundred missionaries were killed, sharpened the question of whether Chinese believers could own their faith. In 1906 Yu Guozhen founded the Chinese Christian Independent Church in Shanghai, and by the 1920s hundreds of self-supporting congregations had joined it. The National Christian Conference of 1922, the founding of the Church of Christ in China (1927) and the anti-Christian movement of 1922–27 made ‘indigenisation’ the watchword of Chinese Protestant leaders such as Cheng Jingyi.

More radical independence came from below. In Beijing in 1917 Wei Enbo, influenced by Pentecostal missionaries, founded the True Jesus Church, Sabbath-keeping, baptising in Jesus’ name and practising tongues and healing. In Shandong, Jing Dianying founded the Jesus Family at Mazhuang in the 1920s, a communal society of shared property and ecstatic worship. In Fuzhou the young Ni Tuosheng (Watchman Nee), shaped by Plymouth Brethren teaching and the missionary Margaret Barber, rejected denominations altogether; his ‘local churches’ (called the Little Flock by others) recognised one church per city, and his writings such as The Spiritual Man and The Normal Christian Life later became evangelical classics in the West. Wang Mingdao’s Christian Tabernacle in Beijing (from 1925) stood for strict biblicism and complete self-support.

Revival gave this movement fire. The Norwegian Lutheran missionary Marie Monsen’s searching preaching helped spark the Shandong Revival (1927–37), with its confession of sin, healings and spiritual gifts. The American-educated chemist John Sung (Song Shangjie), returning in 1927, became China’s most famous evangelist: with the Bethel Worldwide Evangelistic Band from 1931, and then alone, he preached in almost every province and from 1935 among the Chinese of the Philippines, Singapore, Malaya, Siam, Indonesia and Taiwan, leaving behind thousands of witness teams. These revivals planted an evangelical, conversion-centred piety that proved independent of missionaries.

After 1949 the new government required churches to sever foreign ties. The ‘Christian Manifesto’ drafted by Wu Yaozong (Y. T. Wu) with Zhou Enlai’s approval in 1950 launched the Three-Self Patriotic Movement, formally organised in 1954, which borrowed the old missionary slogan of self-government, self-support and self-propagation for a new political purpose. All foreign missionaries had left by the early 1950s. Accusation meetings denounced missionaries and Chinese leaders; Wang Mingdao, refusing to join, was imprisoned from 1955 to 1979; Watchman Nee was arrested in 1952 and died in a labour camp in 1972; Catholic bishops loyal to Rome were jailed. In the Cultural Revolution (1966–76) all public worship ceased, but Christians met secretly in homes, especially in rural Henan, Anhui and Zhejiang.

When churches reopened in 1979 the Christian community was far larger than in 1949, when there had been perhaps 700,000–1 million Protestants. The China Christian Council (1980), led by Bishop K. H. Ting (Ding Guangxun), worked with the Three-Self Movement to reopen churches, train pastors and print Bibles through the Amity Press (from 1987). Alongside it grew vast unregistered networks, among them the Fangcheng fellowship, China Gospel Fellowship, the Born Again movement of Xu Yongze and the house churches of Wenzhou, while urban leaders such as Allen Yuan and Samuel Lamb (Lin Xiangao) in Guangzhou became symbols of faithful endurance. Estimates of Chinese Protestants in the 2010s range from the government’s 38 million (2018) to Pew’s c. 58 million (2010) and higher figures from some advocates, figures that reflect real uncertainty.

The Back to Jerusalem vision began in the 1940s, when Chinese evangelists from the Northwest Bible Institute at Fengxiang and the Jesus Family’s Northwest Spiritual Band set out to evangelise westward through Xinjiang toward the Muslim world and ultimately Jerusalem; their leaders, including Mark Ma and Simon Zhao, were stopped by the Communist victory, and Zhao spent decades in prison. Revived in the 2000s through the books of Brother Yun (Liu Zhenying) and Paul Hattaway, with an announced goal of 100,000 missionaries, the vision has mobilised Chinese mission interest but produced far smaller numbers than proclaimed. Since 2014 the destruction of crosses in Zhejiang, the 2018 Regulations on Religious Affairs, the closure of Beijing’s Zion Church and Chengdu’s Early Rain Covenant Church, and the nine-year sentence given to pastor Wang Yi in 2019 have placed both registered and unregistered churches under heavy pressure.
beliefs: Conservative evangelical theology with strong emphases on the Bible, conversion, holiness and the imminent return of Christ, transmitted by revivalists and indigenous teachers rather than by seminaries.
The principle that Chinese churches must be self-governing, self-supporting and self-propagating, shared in different senses by independent churches, Three-Self and house churches.
In the house churches, the conviction that the church’s head is Christ, not the state, and that suffering is a normal mark of faithfulness.
Watchman Nee’s ecclesiology of one church in each locality and his teaching on the spirit, soul and body and the ‘inner life’.
Pentecostal-type expectations of healing, exorcism, visions and spiritual gifts, widespread in rural networks and in the True Jesus Church.
In the Three-Self Movement, ‘love country, love church’ and K. H. Ting’s project of theological reconstruction emphasising God’s love over the believer–unbeliever divide.
strategies: Self-supporting independent congregations and federations, starting with the Chinese Christian Independent Church in 1906.
Itinerant revival campaigns with evangelistic bands and witness teams that continued after the evangelist left.
Lay-led meetings in homes, with itinerant evangelists, hand-copied Scripture and short-term training classes during times of persecution.
Networks of house churches with their own training schools, sending ‘workers’ from Henan and Anhui to other provinces.
State-registered churches, seminaries and Bible printing (Amity Press) within the framework of the Three-Self Movement.
Overseas Chinese networks in Southeast Asia, Taiwan and North America that carried revival preaching and literature beyond China.
groupsReached: Rural Han Chinese villagers in Henan, Anhui, Shandong and Zhejiang, who became the core of the house-church networks.
Urban intellectuals, students and professionals, among whom ‘urban house churches’ multiplied after the 1990s.
Overseas Chinese in the Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Taiwan through John Sung and other revivalists.
Wenzhou entrepreneurs, whose business networks spread churches across China and to Europe.
Chinese migrant workers in coastal factory cities.
Some minority peoples (Lisu, Miao, Yi) whose churches, founded by missions, became wholly indigenous after 1950.
challenges: The identification of Christianity with Western imperialism, the unequal treaties and the anti-Christian movements of 1900 and 1922–27.
War with Japan and civil war (1937–49), which disrupted churches across the country.
Persecution under Communist rule: accusation campaigns, long imprisonments and the total closure of churches in 1966–79.
The division between registered and unregistered Christians, marked by mutual suspicion and theological disagreement.
A shortage of trained pastors relative to the rapid growth of believers after 1979.
Since 2018, renewed restrictions on online worship, youth ministry, foreign contacts and church buildings.
harms: Three-Self accusation campaigns of the early 1950s compelled Christians to denounce missionaries and fellow believers, leaving lasting wounds and mistrust.
Rival claims of orthodoxy between registered and unregistered churches have led to mutual condemnation and, at times, to reporting fellow Christians to the authorities.
Poorly taught rural networks proved vulnerable to heterodox movements such as Eastern Lightning (Church of Almighty God), which has used deception and coercion against house-church members.
Exaggerated statistics and dramatic testimonies published by some Western advocacy groups distorted perceptions and complicated life for Chinese believers.
Authoritarian leadership and personality cults in some networks and in Witness Lee’s later movement produced divisions and abuse allegations.
developments: Proved that Chinese Christianity could survive and grow without missionaries, foreign funds or public church buildings.
Produced theological and devotional writings, especially Watchman Nee’s, that have shaped evangelicals worldwide.
Created a Chinese Christian hymnody, notably the Canaan Hymns of the house-church songwriter Lü Xiaomin.
Inspired missionary vision among Chinese believers through the Back to Jerusalem movement and overseas Chinese churches.
Showed how revival preaching, lay leadership and home meetings can sustain a church through prolonged persecution.
Through the registered churches, reopened tens of thousands of churches and printed many tens of millions of Bibles inside China.
missions.outcome: Chinese Christianity became thoroughly Chinese in leadership and style and grew from about one million Protestants in 1949 to tens of millions, but remains divided between registered and unregistered churches and under tightening state control.

keyPeople.name: Watchman Nee (Ni Tuosheng)
keyPeople.role: Founder of the Local Churches (‘Little Flock’) and writer
keyPeople.focus: Non-denominational local churches and the inner spiritual life.
keyPeople.outcome: Imprisoned from 1952; died in a labour camp in 1972.

keyPeople.name: John Sung (Song Shangjie)
keyPeople.focus: Repentance-centred revival campaigns across China and Southeast Asia, 1928–1940.
keyPeople.outcome: Died of illness in Beijing in 1944; his witness teams shaped Chinese evangelicalism.

keyPeople.name: Wang Mingdao
keyPeople.focus: Strict biblicism and complete independence from missions and state.
keyPeople.outcome: Imprisoned 1955–1979 for refusing to join the Three-Self Movement.

keyPeople.name: Marie Monsen
keyPeople.focus: Searching preaching on sin and new birth that helped spark the Shandong Revival.
keyPeople.outcome: Her revival reshaped piety in north China.

keyPeople.name: Wu Yaozong (Y. T. Wu)
keyPeople.role: YMCA leader and founder of the Three-Self Patriotic Movement
keyPeople.focus: Drafted the 1950 Christian Manifesto aligning the church with the new state.
keyPeople.outcome: Chaired the Three-Self Movement; criticised by house-church Christians.

keyPeople.name: K. H. Ting (Ding Guangxun)
keyPeople.role: Anglican bishop, head of the China Christian Council
keyPeople.focus: Reopening churches after 1979, Nanjing seminary and the Amity Foundation.
keyPeople.outcome: Led the official Protestant church for three decades.

keyPeople.name: Wei Enbo (Paul Wei)
keyPeople.role: Founder of the True Jesus Church
keyPeople.focus: Sabbath-keeping, Oneness Pentecostal indigenous church founded in 1917.
keyPeople.outcome: The church spread across China, Taiwan and the diaspora.

keyPeople.name: Jing Dianying
keyPeople.focus: Communal Christian living and charismatic worship.
keyPeople.outcome: Imprisoned after 1952; the Family was dissolved.

countries.text: Independent churches from 1906, indigenous movements in Beijing, Shandong and Fujian, the Three-Self churches and the vast post-1979 house-church networks.
The True Jesus Church arrived in 1926; Witness Lee moved the Local Churches’ centre to Taipei in 1949; John Sung preached there in 1936.
John Sung’s campaigns of 1935–39 revived Chinese churches and left lasting evangelistic bands.
Sung’s preaching among Chinese Indonesians in Java and Sumatra founded influential evangelistic movements.
Sung’s campaigns strengthened Chinese churches in Manila and beyond.
Witness Lee moved to Los Angeles in 1962 and founded the Living Stream Ministry; Chinese diaspora churches multiplied.
Back to Jerusalem evangelists reached Urumqi, Hami and Kashgar in the late 1940s before the Communist victory stopped them.
A refuge for Chinese evangelists and publishers after 1949, and later a base for Bible distribution and church support in the mainland.

journeys.title: John Sung’s revival tours of Southeast Asia
journeys.text: Sung’s campaigns among overseas Chinese drew large crowds, emphasised confession of sin and formed small evangelistic bands of converts to continue the work; the stops shown are among many he visited.

journeys.title: The first Back to Jerusalem evangelists head for Xinjiang
journeys.people: Mark Ma, Simon Zhao and members of the Back to Jerusalem Evangelistic Band
journeys.text: Small teams walked and rode along the old Silk Road intending to evangelise westward to Jerusalem; the closing of China’s borders and arrests after 1949 ended the effort, and Simon Zhao spent decades in prison in Xinjiang.

journeys.title: Witness Lee carries the Local Churches to Taiwan
journeys.text: Sent by Watchman Nee to Taiwan as the Communists took Shanghai, Lee built the Local Churches there and later in the United States, while Nee remained and was imprisoned.

relations.text: The Back to Jerusalem vision and overseas Chinese churches made China a potential, if constrained, sending church.
The China Christian Council joined the World Council of Churches in 1991, linking the registered church to the ecumenical movement.
Korean and Chinese-diaspora missionaries supported house-church training and Bible distribution after 1992, often informally.

agreements.text: Adopted (and transformed) Henry Venn’s three-self principle — self-government, self-support and self-propagation — as the charter of Chinese church independence.
House churches largely retained the CIM’s conservative evangelical theology, Chinese dress-and-language identification and expectation of suffering.
Shared the Korean church’s revival piety, early-morning prayer and lay leadership.

disagreements.text: Independent leaders such as Wang Mingdao and Watchman Nee rejected denominational and missionary control, and the Three-Self Movement denounced the CIM and other missions as instruments of imperialism.
House-church Christians criticised the WCC and Western ecumenical bodies for partnering with the state-controlled Three-Self churches while unregistered believers were imprisoned.

Protestant indigenous movements repudiated the Catholic accommodation of ancestor rites, while the Catholic community itself split between the state-sponsored Patriotic Association and the Rome-loyal underground.
The True Jesus Church adopted Pentecostal practice but broke with Western Pentecostal missions, condemning them as false churches and adopting Oneness and Sabbatarian teaching.

deviations: The Three-Self Movement’s political subordination to the Party’s United Front departed from the original missionary meaning of ‘self-government’, which had aimed at freedom from external control.

Witness Lee’s later teachings (e.g. ‘calling on the name of the Lord’ and the ‘mingling’ of God and man) were condemned in China as the ‘Shouters’ and debated as heterodox by evangelicals, though some Western evangelical bodies later affirmed the Local Churches as orthodox.
The True Jesus Church’s Oneness theology and claim to be the only true church diverged from historic Trinitarian Christianity.
Eastern Lightning’s claim that Christ has returned as a Chinese woman represents a complete break from Christianity that exploited house-church networks.

missions.name: Latin American Protestant and Pentecostal growth
missions.statusNote: Active and still growing in most countries: Pew (2014) found about 19% of Latin Americans identifying as Protestant, most of them Pentecostal or charismatic, and Brazil’s 2022 census recorded about 27% evangélicos. Growth has slowed in some countries as the religiously unaffiliated also increase, and evangelicals have become a major political force.
missions.summary: Protestantism entered Catholic Latin America with Bible-sellers, immigrants and nineteenth-century missions, but it became a mass movement only when Latin Americans took it over. The Chilean Methodist revival of 1909 and the Swedish-American founders of Brazil’s Assemblies of God in 1911 began a Pentecostal expansion led overwhelmingly by local, often poor and lay pastors. By the early twenty-first century Latin America had tens of millions of evangelicals, a distinctive evangelical theology of ‘integral mission’, powerful neo-Pentecostal corporations such as the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, and a growing presence in politics — together with fierce controversies over prosperity teaching, religious intolerance and alliances with authoritarian power.
missions.story:
For three centuries the Iberian Patronato and Padroado excluded Protestantism from Latin America. After independence, Bible-society agents such as the Scot James ‘Diego’ Thomson, who promoted Lancasterian schools and Scripture reading in Buenos Aires, Chile, Peru, Colombia and Mexico between 1818 and 1830, found liberal politicians willing to welcome Protestant ideas. Immigrant churches followed (German Lutherans in Brazil from 1824, Welsh in Patagonia from 1865), and then missions: the Scottish doctor Robert Kalley in Rio de Janeiro (1855), the American Presbyterian Ashbel Green Simonton (1859), Southern Methodists and Southern Baptists (W. B. Bagby at Salvador, 1882). Growth was slow and largely middle-class; Edinburgh 1910 even excluded Latin America as already Christian, provoking the separate Panama Congress on Christian Work in Latin America in 1916.

The decisive change came from revival. In 1909 the Methodist congregation of the American missionary Willis Hoover in Valparaíso, Chile, experienced tongues, visions and ecstatic worship; expelled by the Methodist Episcopal Church, Hoover and his Chilean followers formed the Iglesia Metodista Pentecostal in 1910, which multiplied through street preaching by ordinary members. In 1910 two Swedish Baptist immigrants from the United States, Daniel Berg and Gunnar Vingren, arrived in Belém at the mouth of the Amazon; expelled from a Baptist church for their Pentecostal teaching, they founded in 1911 what became the Assembleias de Deus, Brazil’s largest Protestant body. The Italian-American Luigi Francescon founded the Congregação Cristã no Brasil among Italians in São Paulo the same year.

These churches quickly passed into Latin American hands. Their pastors were workers, peasants and migrants rather than seminary graduates; they preached on street corners, held healing campaigns, met in storefronts and spoke the language and music of the poor. Brazil’s second wave in the 1950s–60s — the Foursquare Church’s tent crusades, Manoel de Mello’s O Brasil para Cristo (1955) and David Miranda’s Deus é Amor (1962) — used radio and mass healing meetings. A third, neo-Pentecostal wave followed with Edir Macedo’s Igreja Universal do Reino de Deus, founded in a former funeral parlour in Rio de Janeiro in 1977, and R. R. Soares’s Igreja Internacional da Graça (1980), which combined deliverance from evil spirits, intense fundraising, television and later political parties.

In Central America, Pentecostalism spread rapidly amid civil wars and natural disasters. In Guatemala, Protestants rose to roughly two-fifths of the population by 2014; the evangelical general Efraín Ríos Montt, an elder of the Church of the Word (El Verbo), ruled in 1982–83 during the worst massacres of Maya villages and was convicted of genocide in 2013 before the verdict was annulled. Among the Maya, Quechua, Aymara and Mapuche, evangelical and Pentecostal churches offered literacy, temperance and leadership, but also provoked conflict with Catholic and traditional communities: in San Juan Chamula, Chiapas, thousands of indigenous Protestants were expelled from their villages from the 1970s onward.

Latin American evangelicals also developed their own theology. The first Latin American Congress on Evangelism (CLADE, Bogotá 1969) and the Latin American Theological Fraternity (founded 1970) gathered thinkers such as René Padilla, Samuel Escobar and Orlando Costas, whose ‘misión integral’ insisted that evangelism and social justice belong together. Their interventions at Lausanne 1974 shaped the Lausanne Covenant’s affirmation of social responsibility and challenged North American church-growth pragmatism. Meanwhile Catholic liberation theology and the Catholic Charismatic Renewal competed for the same poor neighbourhoods; it was often said that ‘the Catholic Church opted for the poor, but the poor opted for the Pentecostals’.

By the 2010s Brazil had more Pentecostals than any other country, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua were around 40% Protestant, and Latin American churches were sending missionaries to Portugal, Africa, Japan and the United States. The evangelical vote (the Brazilian ‘bancada evangélica’ in Congress, support for presidents such as Jair Bolsonaro) became a decisive political factor, and critics pointed to prosperity teaching, financial scandals and attacks on Afro-Brazilian religions; defenders highlighted the movement’s role in giving dignity, community and leadership to millions of the poor, and particularly to women.
beliefs: Conversion and personal faith in Christ, in conscious contrast to what evangelicals saw as nominal, sacramental and saint-centred popular Catholicism.
The authority of the Bible, read and preached by lay members in their own words.
Pentecostal baptism in the Holy Spirit, speaking in tongues, divine healing and deliverance from evil spirits.
Strict personal morality — abstinence from alcohol, tobacco, gambling and adultery — which reorganised family economies, especially for women.
In neo-Pentecostal churches, ‘prosperity’ and ‘spiritual warfare’ teaching that links tithes and offerings to God’s material blessing.
In the Latin American Theological Fraternity, ‘integral mission’: the whole gospel for the whole person, uniting evangelism and social justice.
strategies: Street preaching, open-air services and personal testimony by every member, the hallmark of the Chilean Methodist Pentecostals.
Apprenticeship rather than seminary training: pastors rose from the ranks of lay preachers, allowing rapid multiplication of congregations.
Small storefront churches in urban peripheries and rural villages, often within walking distance of members.
Mass healing campaigns, radio from the 1950s and television networks from the 1980s (such as the IURD’s Rede Record, bought in 1989).
Bible translation, literacy and schools among indigenous peoples, often in partnership with SIL/Wycliffe.
Electoral organisation and party-building to defend religious freedom and promote conservative moral policies.
groupsReached: The urban poor and rural migrants of Brazil, Chile, Mexico and Central America.
Women, who formed a majority of members and found in Pentecostal discipline a means to reform husbands and households.
Indigenous peoples such as the Maya of Guatemala and Chiapas, the Quechua and Aymara of the Andes and the Mapuche of Chile.
Afro-Brazilians and Afro-Latin communities, among whom Pentecostal growth has been especially strong.
Prisoners, addicts and gang members, through rehabilitation ministries in Brazil and Central America.
Latin American migrants in the United States, Spain and Portugal, now a major part of evangelical churches there.
challenges: Legal discrimination and Catholic hostility in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, including violence against Protestants in Colombia during La Violencia (1948–58).
Expulsion of early Pentecostals from Methodist and Baptist churches, and division into numerous small denominations.
Lack of theological education, making the churches vulnerable to authoritarian leaders and doctrinal novelty.
Poverty, violence, civil war and dictatorship in many countries where the churches grew.
The tension between integral-mission thinkers and prosperity or politically partisan leaders within the same movement.
Recent losses to secularisation among young people in Chile, Uruguay and other countries.
harms: Prosperity teaching and aggressive fundraising, especially in neo-Pentecostal churches such as the IURD, have extracted money from the poor and led to fraud investigations in several countries.

Attacks on Afro-Brazilian religions — from televised demonisation of Candomblé and Umbanda to vandalism of terreiros — and the 1995 televised kicking of a statue of Our Lady of Aparecida by an IURD bishop fuelled religious intolerance.
Support for authoritarian regimes, most notoriously Ríos Montt’s Guatemala (1982–83), and silence about human-rights abuses by some leaders.
Village conflicts in Chiapas and elsewhere, where both sides used violence, expulsions and property seizures.
Concentration of authority and wealth in founder-bishops and family dynasties, with little accountability.
Some foreign mission agencies working among indigenous peoples were accused of facilitating state or corporate penetration of their lands, leading to the expulsion of SIL from several countries.
developments: Gave millions of poor Latin Americans literacy, community, leadership roles and a sense of dignity independent of patrons and clergy.
Produced a distinctively Latin American evangelical theology — misión integral — that reshaped the Lausanne movement and global evangelical social ethics.
Created the largest national Pentecostal movements in the world, wholly led and financed by Latin Americans.
Contributed to religious freedom and pluralism in historically Catholic states.
Promoted temperance and family stability, which researchers link to improved household welfare among converts.
Turned Latin America into a missionary-sending region, notably through COMIBAM (1987) and Brazilian agencies.
missions.outcome: Latin America changed from an almost exclusively Catholic continent to one where about one person in five is Protestant, mostly Pentecostal, with deep effects on politics, culture and global Christianity.

keyPeople.name: Willis C. Hoover
keyPeople.role: Methodist missionary, founder of Chilean Pentecostalism
keyPeople.focus: Led the 1909 Valparaíso revival and the Iglesia Metodista Pentecostal.
keyPeople.outcome: Expelled from the Methodist Episcopal Church; his church grew under Chilean leadership.

keyPeople.name: Daniel Berg
keyPeople.role: Co-founder of the Assembleias de Deus in Brazil
keyPeople.focus: Colportage and evangelism along the Amazon.
keyPeople.outcome: The church became Brazil’s largest Protestant denomination.

keyPeople.name: Gunnar Vingren
keyPeople.role: Co-founder of the Assembleias de Deus
keyPeople.focus: Pastoral leadership in Belém and Rio de Janeiro.
keyPeople.outcome: Returned to Sweden in 1932; Brazilian leaders took over.

keyPeople.name: Manoel de Mello
keyPeople.role: Founder of O Brasil para Cristo
keyPeople.focus: Mass healing and radio evangelism among migrants to São Paulo.
keyPeople.outcome: His church joined the World Council of Churches in 1969, unusually for a Pentecostal body.

keyPeople.name: Edir Macedo
keyPeople.origin: Rio das Flores, Rio de Janeiro
keyPeople.role: Founder of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God
keyPeople.focus: Neo-Pentecostal deliverance, prosperity teaching and media ownership.
keyPeople.outcome: Built a transnational church and media empire amid repeated legal controversies.

keyPeople.name: C. René Padilla
keyPeople.role: Theologian, co-founder of the Latin American Theological Fraternity
keyPeople.focus: Integral mission and critique of North American church-growth methods.
keyPeople.outcome: Decisively shaped Lausanne 1974 and global evangelical social ethics.

keyPeople.name: Samuel Escobar
keyPeople.focus: Evangelism and social responsibility; mission from the global South.
keyPeople.outcome: Key voice at Lausanne 1974 and in the International Fellowship of Evangelical Students.

keyPeople.name: James ‘Diego’ Thomson
keyPeople.focus: Lancasterian schools and Bible distribution in newly independent republics.
keyPeople.outcome: Prepared the way for later Protestant presence.

countries.text: From Kalley’s church (1855) to the Assemblies of God (1911) and the IURD (1977), Brazil became the world’s largest Pentecostal nation; the 2022 census recorded about 27% evangelicals.
The Valparaíso revival of 1909 created an autonomous Pentecostal movement that grew to perhaps a sixth of the population by the late twentieth century.
Presbyterian mission from 1882; rapid Pentecostal growth after the 1976 earthquake made Guatemala around 40% Protestant by 2014.
Liberal reforms admitted Protestant missions in the 1870s; Pentecostal and indigenous Protestant growth has been strongest in Chiapas and the south.
Thomson’s schools and later immigrant churches; the healing campaigns of Tommy Hicks (1954) and the 1980s–90s revival under Carlos Annacondia stimulated Pentecostal growth.
Evangelical work among Quechua and Aymara; Samuel Escobar and evangelical students; the evangelical vote mattered in the 1990 election of Alberto Fujimori.
Presbyterians from 1856; Protestants were persecuted during La Violencia (1948–58) but grew rapidly after the 1991 constitution guaranteed religious freedom.
Moravian work on the Miskito coast from 1849 and later Pentecostal growth brought both countries to around 40% Protestant by 2014.
Evangelical missions, radio (HCJB in Quito, 1931) and indigenous Quechua churches transformed highland communities.

journeys.title: Diego Thomson’s Bible and school journeys through the new republics
journeys.text: Welcomed by independence leaders such as San Martín and Bolívar’s governments, Thomson set up Lancasterian schools using Bible texts as readers and distributed Spanish Scriptures for the British and Foreign Bible Society.

journeys.title: Berg and Vingren sail to Belém
journeys.text: After a prophecy that they were to go to ‘Pará’, the two Swedes sailed from New York and arrived in Belém on 19 November 1910; in June 1911 they and a small group of Baptists expelled with them formed the Apostolic Faith Mission, renamed Assembleia de Deus in 1918.

relations.text: Brazilian and other Latin American churches became major missionary senders, organised through COMIBAM from 1987.
Latin American theologians shaped the Lausanne Covenant’s affirmation of social responsibility and the later language of integral mission.
A minority of Latin American Pentecostal churches (Iglesia Pentecostal de Chile, O Brasil para Cristo) joined the World Council of Churches in the 1960s.

agreements.text: Shared the Azusa-era emphases on Spirit baptism, healing and lay evangelism, though Latin American churches soon became autonomous.
Valued vernacular Scripture, literacy and indigenous-language ministry among Maya and Andean peoples.
Affirmed evangelism as primary while insisting with the Lausanne Covenant that social and political involvement are part of Christian duty.

disagreements.text: Defined itself against the colonial Catholic monopoly and popular Catholic devotion to saints, provoking reciprocal Catholic hostility until well after Vatican II.
Resented Edinburgh 1910’s exclusion of Latin America as already Christian; most Pentecostals later rejected the WCC as liberal and too close to Rome.
Padilla and Escobar criticised the homogeneous unit principle and managerial church-growth techniques as culturally North American and theologically thin.
Chilean Pentecostals were expelled from the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1910 for ‘unscriptural and irrational’ practices.

deviations: Neo-Pentecostal prosperity teaching, which treats offerings as investments in divine blessing, departs from the early Pentecostals’ ascetic and other-worldly piety and from wider Christian teaching on poverty.
Some churches adopted ritual objects (anointed oil, salt, roses, ‘holy’ water) and ‘unloading’ sessions that critics see as reproducing the magical practices they condemned in popular religion.
Political projects aiming at evangelical dominion or partisan alignment contradict the early movement’s refusal of worldly power and its defence of a secular state.
Founder-bishops ruling as unaccountable owners of their churches departed from the Pentecostal ideal of the priesthood of all believers.

missions.name: Majority-world sending movements (Nigeria, Brazil, India, Philippines; ‘from everywhere to everywhere’)
missions.statusNote: Active and expanding: by around 2010 Brazil, South Korea and India were among the ten largest sending countries, and much of the world’s missionary force now comes from Africa, Asia and Latin America — though many majority-world workers serve within their own countries or diasporas, and statistics remain uncertain.
missions.summary: In the twentieth century the churches planted by Western missions — and many that arose independently — began to send missionaries of their own, first to neighbouring peoples and then across the world. Indian, Nigerian, Ghanaian, Brazilian, Korean, Filipino and Chinese Christians built agencies, denominational mission boards and migrant church networks, so that by the early twenty-first century mission was, in Michael Nazir-Ali’s phrase, ‘from everywhere to everywhere’. The movement brought cultural closeness, lower costs and fresh energy, and challenged the assumption that mission meant the West going to the rest; it also reproduced some old problems and exported new ones, notably prosperity teaching.
missions.story:
Non-Western Christians had always carried the faith — Pacific Islander teachers in the nineteenth century, African catechists, Bishop Crowther’s Niger Mission, Korean missionaries to Shandong in 1913 — but organised majority-world sending as a self-conscious movement began in India. In 1903 Tamil Christians in Tirunelveli formed the Indian Missionary Society, sending V. S. Azariah to the Telugu-speaking Dornakal area in 1909; in 1905 the National Missionary Society was founded at Serampore with the motto ‘Indian men, Indian money, Indian leadership’. Azariah’s speech at Edinburgh 1910 — ‘Give us friends!’ — became a classic protest against missionary paternalism.

After decolonisation the call for self-reliance grew sharper. In 1971 the Kenyan Presbyterian John Gatu proposed a moratorium on Western missionaries and funds so that African churches could find their own identity, a debate taken up at the WCC’s Bangkok conference (1973) and the All Africa Conference of Churches (1974). Evangelicals answered differently, by mobilising non-Western missionaries: Lausanne 1974 gave majority-world leaders such as René Padilla, Samuel Escobar and Festo Kivengere a global platform, and associations multiplied — the Evangelical Missionary Society of ECWA in Nigeria (1948), Calvary Ministries (CAPRO, 1975) and the Nigeria Evangelical Missions Association (1982); the Indian Evangelical Mission (1965), Friends Missionary Prayer Band (1958) and India Missions Association (1977); the Philippine Missions Association (1983); and COMIBAM, whose 1987 congress in São Paulo declared that Latin America had moved ‘from mission field to mission force’.

Indian mission is the largest and most distinctive branch: tens of thousands of Indian workers, mostly from the Christian south and northeast, serve cross-culturally among other language groups in north India, a form of mission that is foreign in culture but domestic in geography. In Nigeria and Ghana, denominational churches such as the Redeemed Christian Church of God (founded 1952; led from 1981 by Enoch Adeboye), Deeper Life Bible Church, Winners’ Chapel and Ghana’s Church of Pentecost planted congregations across Africa and among the diaspora; the RCCG claims parishes in well over a hundred countries. Brazilian Baptists, Assemblies of God and the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God followed Portuguese-speaking links to Angola, Mozambique and Portugal, and Brazilian missionaries went to Japan among Japanese-Brazilian migrants and to the Muslim world.

Migration became a mission strategy in its own right. Filipino domestic workers, nurses and seamen — millions of overseas Filipino workers — formed churches in the Gulf, Hong Kong and Europe, and Filipino agencies trained them as ‘tentmakers’. African-led churches became the largest congregations in London (Kingsway International Christian Centre, founded 1992 by the Nigerian Matthew Ashimolowo), while the Nigerian pastor Sunday Adelaja founded the Embassy of the Blessed Kingdom of God for All Nations in Kyiv in 1994, at its height one of Europe’s largest churches. Scholars such as Andrew Walls, Lamin Sanneh, Jehu Hanciles and Kwame Bediako argued that the centre of gravity of Christianity had shifted south, and that ‘reverse mission’ to secular Europe was a real if partial phenomenon — most migrant congregations remain largely ethnic.

The Center for the Study of Global Christianity estimated around 400,000 international missionaries in 2010, with the United States still the largest sender (about 127,000), followed by Brazil (about 34,000) and several European countries and South Korea (about 20,000 each), with India in the top ten. Lausanne’s third congress in Cape Town (2010) and fourth in Incheon (2024) were shaped by majority-world leadership. Critics have noted that the new missions sometimes reproduced Western faults — denominational competition, dependency on foreign funds, ethnocentrism and neglect of member care — and that some exported prosperity and ‘Word of Faith’ teaching or authoritarian ‘big man’ leadership, while defenders stress their cultural nearness, simplicity and willingness to work among the poor and in hostile contexts.
beliefs: The Great Commission is binding on every church, not only on Western churches, and a ‘mission field’ church is not mature until it sends missionaries.
Mission should be from everywhere to everywhere, including to secularised Europe and North America.
Evangelical convictions about conversion, the Bible and the uniqueness of Christ, often combined with Pentecostal expectations of healing, power and spiritual warfare.
The dignity and capacity of non-Western Christians to lead, theologise and fund mission without foreign control.
Holistic mission (integral mission) linking evangelism with education, health and justice, particularly in Latin American and African voices.
In some neo-Pentecostal networks, prosperity and ‘dominion’ teaching that frames mission as conquest of territories and spheres of society.
strategies: National missionary societies funded by local giving, such as the Indian Missionary Society (1903) and National Missionary Society (1905).
Denominational mission boards and church-planting networks that open branches wherever members migrate (RCCG, Church of Pentecost, Assemblies of God).
Prayer-band and support-group models in which ordinary church members pledge regular support for a missionary family (FMPB).
Tentmaking and diaspora mission through migrant workers, students and professionals.
National and continental mission associations (NEMA, IMA, PMA, COMIBAM, KWMA) for training, research and coordination.
Cross-cultural mission within large multilingual nations, especially India, Nigeria and Indonesia.
groupsReached: North Indian Hindi-belt communities, Adivasis and Dalits, reached by South Indian and Northeastern Indian missionaries.
Muslim-majority peoples of northern Nigeria, the Sahel and North Africa, reached by Nigerian and Ghanaian agencies.
Lusophone Africa and Portugal, through Brazilian churches and agencies.
Japanese-Brazilians in Japan and Brazilian migrants worldwide.
Gulf-state migrant communities and East Asian domestic workers, through Filipino churches.
Secularised populations of Western Europe and post-Soviet Eastern Europe through African-led churches.
challenges: Limited funds and currency weakness, making overseas work expensive and missionaries financially insecure.
Visa restrictions, anti-conversion laws and persecution in many receiving countries.
Inadequate training and pastoral care, leading to high attrition and burnout.
Dependence on Western agencies or funding in some cases, raising questions of autonomy.
Ethnic insularity of diaspora churches, which often struggle to reach the host population.
The tension between growth-focused strategies and integral, culturally sensitive mission.
harms: Export of prosperity and Word of Faith teaching from some Nigerian, Ghanaian, Brazilian and Korean churches, encouraging exploitative giving and spiritual manipulation.
Reproduction of denominational rivalry, ethnocentrism and paternalism toward the peoples served — critiques once made of Western missions.
Authoritarian ‘big man’ leadership and financial scandals in some transnational churches, such as the Ukrainian investigations surrounding Sunday Adelaja’s associates in 2008.
Aggressive evangelism that has inflamed communal tensions in India, Nigeria and elsewhere and has been used by opponents to justify anti-conversion laws.
Witchcraft and deliverance teaching carried into diaspora settings, linked in a few notorious cases to the abuse of children accused of witchcraft.
developments: Ended the identification of Christian mission with the West and with colonial power.
Brought missionaries culturally and economically closer to the peoples they serve, often at lower cost.
Produced majority-world missiology (Azariah, Padilla, Escobar, Bediako, Sanneh, Walls’ African colleagues) that reshaped global mission thinking.
Revitalised Christianity in European cities through migrant churches.
Created new forms of mission partnership and research, such as national mission associations and the Lausanne movement’s global networks.
Gave dignity and agency to non-Western Christians as givers, not merely receivers, in the world church.
missions.outcome: By the 2020s most of the world’s Christians and a large and growing share of its missionaries lived in Africa, Asia and Latin America, and global mission had become a polycentric, multidirectional movement.

keyPeople.name: V. S. Azariah
keyPeople.role: Co-founder of the Indian Missionary Society; first Indian Anglican bishop (Dornakal, 1912)
keyPeople.focus: Indian-led mission and mass-movement churches among Telugu Dalits.
keyPeople.outcome: His plea at Edinburgh 1910 for friendship rather than paternalism became famous.

keyPeople.name: John Gatu
keyPeople.role: Moderator of the Presbyterian Church of East Africa
keyPeople.focus: Called in 1971 for a moratorium on Western missionaries and money.
keyPeople.outcome: Sparked a global debate on dependency and self-reliance.

keyPeople.name: Enoch Adejare Adeboye
keyPeople.role: General Overseer of the Redeemed Christian Church of God from 1981
keyPeople.focus: Transnational church-planting with the aim of a church within reach of every person.
