keyPeople.outcome: Made the RCCG one of the most widespread African churches worldwide.

keyPeople.name: Kwame Bediako
keyPeople.role: Theologian and founder of the Akrofi-Christaller Institute
keyPeople.focus: African Christian identity and the non-Western character of Christianity.
keyPeople.outcome: Shaped the theological understanding of majority-world Christianity.

keyPeople.name: Sunday Adelaja
keyPeople.role: Founder of the Embassy of God, Kyiv (1994)
keyPeople.focus: Charismatic church-planting and social ministry in Ukraine.
keyPeople.outcome: Built one of Europe’s largest congregations, later marred by financial controversy.

keyPeople.name: Matthew Ashimolowo
keyPeople.role: Founder of Kingsway International Christian Centre, London (1992)
keyPeople.focus: African-led Pentecostal church in Britain.
keyPeople.outcome: KICC became one of the largest churches in Britain; criticised by the Charity Commission in 2005 over finances.

countries.text: The Indian Missionary Society (1903), National Missionary Society (1905), FMPB, IEM and the India Missions Association made India one of the largest sources of cross-cultural missionaries, mostly serving within India.
The Evangelical Missionary Society (1948), CAPRO (1975), NEMA (1982) and transnational churches such as the RCCG, Deeper Life and Winners’ Chapel sent workers across Africa and to the diaspora.
The Church of Pentecost, rooted in James McKeown’s work from 1937 and Ghanaian-led since 1982, planted branches in over a hundred countries.
The Brazilian Baptist Junta de Missões Mundiais (1907), COMIBAM (1987) and Pentecostal churches made Brazil one of the top missionary senders.
The Philippine Missions Association (1983) mobilised overseas Filipino workers as tentmakers in the Gulf, Asia and Europe.
Korea’s missionary force grew from under a hundred in 1979 to about 20,000 in the 2010s.
African-led churches such as KICC (1992) and the RCCG became among the largest and fastest-growing congregations in London.
Sunday Adelaja’s Embassy of God in Kyiv became a symbol of African ‘reverse mission’ to Europe.
John Gatu’s call for a moratorium on missionaries began a continental debate on self-reliance.
Brazilian Pentecostal and neo-Pentecostal churches expanded after independence, using the Portuguese language and media.

journeys.title: V. S. Azariah goes to Dornakal for the Indian Missionary Society
journeys.text: Tamil Christians funded and sent their own missionary to the Telugu-speaking Nizam’s territory; Azariah was consecrated in 1912 as Bishop of Dornakal, the first Indian bishop of the Anglican communion.

journeys.title: Sunday Adelaja from Nigeria to Kyiv
journeys.text: Adelaja went to the Soviet Union to study journalism in Minsk, became a Christian worker after the collapse of communism, and in 1994 founded the church in Kyiv that became an emblem of ‘reverse mission’.

journeys.title: The Lausanne congresses move south and east
journeys.text: The movement’s four global congresses traced the shift of evangelical mission leadership toward Asia and Africa.

relations.text: Majority-world agencies and leaders became the centre of Lausanne’s networks from Manila 1989 onwards.
Pacific churches such as the Tongan, Samoan and Fijian Methodists and Congregationalists continue a long tradition of Islander sending within the modern movement.

agreements.text: Shared the priority of evangelism, the unreached-peoples focus and the integration of social responsibility affirmed in the Lausanne Covenant.
Fulfilled Venn’s goal of churches that are not only self-supporting and self-governing but self-propagating, sending missionaries themselves.
Shared the post-colonial critique of paternalism and the call, voiced from Azariah to Gatu, for genuine partnership between older and younger churches.

disagreements.text: Most majority-world evangelical agencies rejected the 1970s moratorium proposal and the WCC’s emphasis on dialogue in favour of active evangelism and church-planting.
Majority-world missiologists criticised Western strategic metrics, ‘closure’ language and managerial missiology as culturally foreign and reductive.
Hosts in Africa, Asia and Latin America have questioned whether Western short-term trips create dependency and serve visitors more than local churches.

deviations: Prosperity and Word of Faith teaching in some sending churches departs from the self-sacrificial vision of early indigenous mission societies like the IMS and NMS.
Some transnational churches serve chiefly their own diaspora and denominational expansion rather than cross-cultural evangelism, diverging from the ‘everywhere to everywhere’ ideal.
Dependence on Western money in some agencies contradicts the founding principle of self-support (‘Indian men, Indian money’).
Territorial spiritual-warfare and dominion theologies in some networks go beyond mainstream evangelical teaching.

missions.name: Pacific Islander missionaries (Tahitian, Tongan, Fijian, Samoan teachers)
missions.statusNote: Transformed: the nineteenth-century pattern of Islander ‘teachers’ sent under European missionary oversight ended with the autonomy of Pacific churches in the mid-twentieth century, but Tongan, Samoan, Fijian and Cook Islands churches remain missionary-minded and the Pacific is now one of the world’s most Christian regions.
missions.summary: Most of the Pacific was evangelised not by Europeans but by Pacific Islanders. From 1821, Tahitian and Raiatean converts of the London Missionary Society carried Christianity to the Cook Islands and Samoa; Rarotongans and Samoans then went to the Loyalty Islands, New Caledonia, Vanuatu, Tuvalu and Papua; Tongan Methodists took the faith to Fiji, and Fijians, Samoans and Tongans pioneered Methodist missions in New Britain and Papua. Many hundreds of these ‘teachers’ and their wives lived among unfamiliar peoples, learned their languages and often died of disease or violence, while receiving less pay, status and recognition than the European missionaries who supervised them.
missions.story:
The London Missionary Society’s ship Duff landed missionaries in Tahiti in 1797, but the mission made little headway until the chief Pomare II turned to Christianity during civil war, defeating his rivals in 1815 and being baptised in 1819. Converts in Tahiti and Raiatea quickly took the gospel further. In 1821 the Raiatean Papeiha and his companion Vahapata were left on Aitutaki in the Cook Islands by John Williams; in 1823 Papeiha landed on Rarotonga, where within a few years the island’s chiefs had accepted Christianity. Other Tahitian teachers went to the Austral Islands, and in 1830 Williams and Charles Barff, sailing in the locally built Messenger of Peace with eight Tahitian and Raiatean teachers, reached Sapapali’i on Savai’i, where the high chief Malietoa Vainu’upo welcomed them. Samoa became largely Christian within a decade.

The Samoan and Rarotongan churches became sending churches in their turn. From the 1830s and 1840s they sent teachers westward to the Loyalty Islands, New Caledonia, the New Hebrides (Vanuatu), Niue, Tuvalu, Tokelau and Kiribati. The Rarotongan Ta’unga, who worked in New Caledonia from 1842 to 1845 and wrote a remarkable account of his experiences, exemplifies their courage and their ethnographic eye. Many were killed — John Williams himself died with Islander companions on Erromango in 1839 — or died of malaria in Melanesia. The LMS training institutions at Takamoa in Rarotonga (1839) and Malua in Samoa (1844) prepared pastors and missionaries.

In Tonga, Wesleyan Methodism took root after 1826 and was adopted by the warrior chief Tāufa’āhau, baptised in 1831 as George, who united Tonga by 1845 and reigned as King George Tupou I. Tongan Christians reached Lakeba in Fiji before the first Wesleyan missionaries, William Cross and David Cargill, landed there in 1835, and Tongan teachers such as Joeli Bulu (in Fiji from 1838 until his death in 1877) became the backbone of the Fijian mission. The conversion of the Bau chief Cakobau in 1854 — supported by Tongan political power — opened Fiji to Methodism. Fijian Christians in turn went to New Britain and New Ireland with George Brown in 1875; several Fijian teachers were killed there in 1878. Fijians, Samoans and Tongans pioneered the Methodist mission in Papua’s Dobu region from 1891.

The ‘Coming of the Light’ to the Torres Strait and Papua also depended on Islanders. On 1 July 1871 the LMS missionaries Samuel Macfarlane and A. W. Murray landed Loyalty Islander teachers on Erub (Darnley Island), an event still celebrated as a public holiday in the Torres Strait. Rarotongan, Samoan and Niuean teachers followed along the Papuan coast; the Rarotongan Ruatoka served at Port Moresby from the early 1870s until his death in 1903 and was remembered by Papuans and Europeans alike as a pastor of great courage. In the Anglican Melanesian Mission, Melanesian converts trained on Norfolk Island became teachers and priests, and in 1925 the Solomon Islander Ini Kopuria founded the Melanesian Brotherhood, an indigenous religious order of evangelists.

Islander mission had a shadow side. Teachers were paid a fraction of European salaries and rarely ordained or credited; histories long named the European missionary and not the Tahitian or Samoan who had actually lived in the village. Polynesian teachers sometimes looked down on Melanesians, imposed Polynesian dress and customs, and acted as local agents of chiefly or missionary power. Christian chiefs enacted law codes — the Vava’u Code of 1839 in Tonga and the ‘blue laws’ of the Cook Islands — enforcing Sabbath observance, dress and sexual morality with fines and punishment. Conversion was often bound up with war and chiefly politics, as in Tonga and Fiji, and Christianity was the occasion for the destruction of marae, carvings and religious objects.

In the twentieth century the churches became autonomous: the Samoan LMS church became self-governing (formally independent in 1962), the Methodist Church in Fiji in 1964, and the Pacific Conference of Churches (first conference at Malua, 1961; formally constituted 1966) and the Pacific Theological College in Suva (1966) gave the region its own ecumenical and theological institutions. Pacific churches continue to send pastors and missionaries to their diasporas in New Zealand, Australia and the United States, and to Papua New Guinea and beyond, while Pentecostal and evangelical movements have created new patterns of Islander mission.
beliefs: Evangelical Protestant faith — conversion, the Bible, Sabbath observance and the overthrow of the old gods — as taught by the LMS and Wesleyan missionaries.
The conviction that God had given the new Christian islands a duty to carry the ‘light’ to peoples still in ‘darkness’, often expressed in strong biblical and covenantal language.
Strict Sabbath keeping, modest dress and the reform of sexual and marriage customs as visible signs of the new order.
Honour for chiefs and communal decision-making, adapted to church life so that whole villages and lineages joined together.
Willingness to suffer and die for the gospel, which Islander churches commemorated in their memory of martyred teachers.
strategies: Placing Islander teachers and their wives in villages, often alone, to live, learn the language and gain chiefly protection ahead of European missionaries.
Use of mission ships (Messenger of Peace, Camden, John Williams, Southern Cross) to carry teachers across the ocean and supply them.
Training colleges such as Takamoa (Rarotonga, 1839), Malua (Samoa, 1844) and Navuloa (Fiji) to prepare pastors and missionaries.
Bible translation and printing in Polynesian and Melanesian languages, with Islanders as key translators.
Working through chiefs, whose conversion often led to the conversion of entire communities.
Church-funded mission through annual contributions (such as Fijian and Samoan missionary meetings), making the islands financially part of the mission.
groupsReached: Cook Islanders, Samoans and other Polynesians through Tahitian and Raiatean teachers.
Fijians, through Tongan Methodist teachers such as Joeli Bulu.
Kanak peoples of New Caledonia and the Loyalty Islands, through Rarotongan and Samoan teachers.
Ni-Vanuatu of the New Hebrides, where many teachers died from malaria or violence.
Torres Strait Islanders and coastal Papuans, through Loyalty Islander, Rarotongan and Samoan teachers from 1871.
Peoples of New Britain, New Ireland and the Papuan islands, through Fijian, Samoan and Tongan Methodists.
challenges: Malaria and other diseases in Melanesia, which killed many Polynesian teachers and their families.
Violence and hostility, including killings of teachers in Vanuatu, New Britain and Papua.
Linguistic and cultural distance between Polynesian teachers and Melanesian peoples.
Isolation, poverty and dependence on irregular visits by mission ships.
Competition with French Catholic missions and colonial power in Tahiti, Wallis and Futuna, and New Caledonia.
Subordination to European missionaries who controlled ordination, funds and the writing of mission history.
harms: Islander teachers were paid far less than Europeans, rarely ordained before the late nineteenth century and largely written out of mission histories.
Mission-inspired law codes, enforced by Christian chiefs, imposed fines and punishment for Sabbath-breaking, dress and sexual offences, and curtailed traditional dance and tattooing.
Conversion became entangled with chiefly warfare in Tahiti, Tonga and Fiji, where victory was taken as proof of the Christian God.
Sacred sites, images and objects were destroyed, and Polynesian customs were sometimes imposed on Melanesian converts as if they were Christian.
In Tonga, the Free Church schism of 1885 led to persecution of Wesleyans loyal to the old church with royal backing.
developments: Evangelised much of Polynesia and Melanesia, making Pacific Islanders among the most Christian peoples in the world.
Showed in the early nineteenth century that newly converted peoples could become missionary-sending churches within a generation.
Produced Bible translations, literacy and printed literature in dozens of Pacific languages.
Left an Islander literature of mission, such as the writings of Ta’unga and the autobiography of Joeli Bulu.
Built theological colleges and the Pacific Conference of Churches, which give Pacific Christianity its own leadership and voice.
Created a lasting tradition of Pacific mission among diaspora and neighbouring peoples.
missions.outcome: Christianity in the Pacific was largely carried by Pacific Islanders themselves, and the churches they founded became self-governing, deeply rooted national institutions, though their pioneers have only recently received due recognition.

keyPeople.name: Papeiha
keyPeople.focus: Pioneer evangelist of Aitutaki (1821) and Rarotonga (1823).
keyPeople.outcome: Served in the Cook Islands for over forty years; honoured as the apostle of Rarotonga.

keyPeople.name: Ta’unga
keyPeople.focus: Mission in New Caledonia (1842–45) and later Samoa.
keyPeople.outcome: His written accounts are a rare Islander record of nineteenth-century mission.

keyPeople.name: Ruatoka
keyPeople.focus: Pastoral work and evangelism at Port Moresby from the early 1870s.
keyPeople.outcome: Remembered as one of the most respected figures of the Papuan mission.

keyPeople.name: Joeli Bulu
keyPeople.focus: Teaching and pastoral leadership in Fiji from 1838.
keyPeople.outcome: His autobiography, published in English in 1871, describes his life as an Islander missionary.

keyPeople.name: George Tupou I (Tāufa’āhau)
keyPeople.role: Methodist convert and king of Tonga
keyPeople.focus: Unified Tonga under a Christian monarchy and supported mission to Fiji.
keyPeople.outcome: Gave Tonga its 1875 constitution; Methodism became the national church.

keyPeople.name: John Williams
keyPeople.focus: Placing Islander teachers across eastern and central Polynesia.
keyPeople.outcome: Killed on Erromango in 1839.

keyPeople.name: Ini Kopuria
keyPeople.focus: An indigenous Anglican order of evangelists living in community.
keyPeople.outcome: The Brotherhood remains active in the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and Papua New Guinea.

countries.text: Base of the LMS mission and of the first Islander teachers after Pomare II’s conversion; French annexation brought Catholic competition from the 1840s.
Evangelised by Papeiha and other Raiatean teachers from 1821; Rarotonga then sent many missionaries westward.
Reached by Tahitian teachers in 1830; the Samoan church, with its Malua college (1844), became the largest LMS sending church in the Pacific.
Wesleyan Methodism took root after 1826 and became the faith of King George Tupou I; Tongans carried it to Fiji.
Tongan Christians and Wesleyan missionaries arrived at Lakeba in 1835; Fiji’s Methodist church later sent missionaries to New Britain and Papua.

countries.country: New Caledonia and the Loyalty Islands
countries.text: Rarotongan and Samoan teachers worked here from the 1840s; Loyalty Islanders later became missionaries to Papua.
Samoan and Rarotongan teachers suffered heavy losses from disease and violence after Williams’s death on Erromango.
Converted largely through Samoan pastors, who remained central to church life into the twentieth century.

countries.country: Papua New Guinea and the Torres Strait
countries.text: The ‘Coming of the Light’ on Erub (1871) and Islander teachers along the Papuan coast; Fijian, Samoan and Tongan Methodists in New Britain (1875) and Dobu (1891).
The Anglican Melanesian Mission trained Melanesian teachers; the indigenous Melanesian Brotherhood was founded in 1925.

journeys.title: Papeiha to Aitutaki and Rarotonga
journeys.text: Left on Aitutaki by Williams in 1821, Papeiha won the island’s chiefs within two years and then landed on Rarotonga in 1823, where he remained for most of his life.

journeys.title: The Messenger of Peace carries Tahitian teachers to Samoa
journeys.people: John Williams, Charles Barff and eight Tahitian and Raiatean teachers
journeys.text: Welcomed by Malietoa Vainu’upo in August 1830, the Tahitian teachers began the work that made Samoa Christian within about a decade.

journeys.title: Tongan Methodists carry the faith to Fiji
journeys.people: Tongan teachers including Joeli Bulu, with William Cross and David Cargill
journeys.text: Tongan Christians, already present in the Lau group, prepared the way for the Wesleyan missionaries and became the mainstay of the Fijian mission until Cakobau of Bau accepted Christianity in 1854.

journeys.title: The ‘Coming of the Light’ to the Torres Strait and Papua
journeys.people: Loyalty Islander teachers with Samuel Macfarlane and A. W. Murray; later Ruatoka
journeys.text: Loyalty Islander teachers landed on Erub on 1 July 1871; within about two years Islander teachers, among them Ruatoka, were established on the Papuan mainland at Port Moresby.

journeys.title: Fijian and Samoan Methodists to New Britain
journeys.people: George Brown with Fijian and Samoan teachers
journeys.text: Fijian volunteers, told they might die, famously replied that they were ready to go; in 1878 a Fijian minister and three Fijian teachers were killed on New Britain.

relations.text: The LMS supplied ships, training and oversight; Islander teachers did most of the pioneering evangelism.
An early precedent for non-Western sending churches, continued today by Pacific churches among their diasporas and neighbours.

agreements.text: Shared the LMS’s evangelical faith, Sabbath discipline and Congregational church order, and its goal of Islander-led churches.
Tongan and Fijian Methodists adopted Wesleyan class meetings, hymn-singing and revival piety, adapted to chiefly society.
Islander teachers were indispensable translators, and vernacular Bibles became treasured national books in Samoa, Tonga, Fiji and the Cook Islands.

disagreements.text: Islander teachers and later Pacific church leaders resented low pay, lack of ordination and European control, which delayed full autonomy until the mid-twentieth century.
Protestant Islander churches clashed with French Catholic missions (Marists from 1836) in Tahiti, Wallis and Futuna and New Caledonia, where religious rivalry was entangled with French annexation.

deviations: The use of chiefly law codes and fines to enforce Christian morality departed from the voluntary conversion the missions professed.
Polynesian teachers sometimes imposed their own cultural norms on Melanesians as if they were Christian requirements.
In Tonga the Free Church of Tonga (1885), created by Shirley Baker and the king to sever ties with the Australasian Methodist conference, persecuted those who stayed loyal to the Wesleyans.
